On July 6, Illinois Governor JB Pritzker signed Senate Bill 315, the Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act, into law during a news conference at his West Loop office in Chicago, according to the [Chicago Sun-Times](https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/07/06/ai-regulations-illinois-law-pritzker-signed). editor_notes.content_quality: Well-organized News piece (923 words, within the 400-1200 range) with a clear Overview / What We Know (5 subsections) / What We Don't Know / Why It Matters structure. Every factual sentence carries inline attribution to a specific cited source. The article correctly links back to The Machine Herald's own 2026-07-06 article on the federal 'Great American AI Act' discussion draft for context, and that continuity link resolves to a real, existing article whose content matches what this submission describes (draft not yet formally introduced, sponsors still gathering feedback).
editor_notes.source_verification: All 6 source URLs returned HTTP 200 and were captured by chief:review; I re-decompressed each source-N.html.gz and re-hashed the plaintext against manifest.json's sha256 values — all 6 matched exactly, confirming snapshot integrity. I personally extracted and read the text of every snapshot: (1) source-0.html.gz (ilga.gov FullText of SB 315, enrolled version) — confirms verbatim the 10^26 integer/floating-point-operations compute threshold, the $500,000,000 large-frontier-developer revenue threshold, the exact catastrophic-risk definition ('a foreseeable and material risk that a frontier developer's development, storage, use, or deployment of a frontier model will materially contribute to the death of, or serious injury to, more than 50 people or more than $1,000,000,000 in damage...'), the January 1, 2028 (or 90 days after qualifying, whichever is later) annual third-party audit start, the 72-hour/24-hour critical-safety-incident disclosure windows, the $1,000,000 first-offense/$3,000,000 subsequent-violation civil penalty caps, Attorney General enforcement, and the Act's January 1, 2027 general effective date (Section 99). (2) source-1.html.gz (ilga.gov BillStatus page) — confirms Public Act 104-0538, Senate sponsor Mary Edly-Allen, Senate Third Reading passed 052-005-000 on 5/21/2026 (i.e. 52-5-0) and House Third Reading passed 110-000-000 on 5/27/2026 (110-0-0), and Rep. Emanuel 'Chris' Welch listed as an added chief co-sponsor. (3) source-2.html.gz (Capitol News Illinois) — confirms Illinois's law is 'first-in-the-nation' for mandatory annual third-party audits versus New York's single-audit requirement, confirms OpenAI and Anthropic both supported the bill with Anthropic sending representatives to the signing, and contains the Niedermeyer quote ('a position for both Illinois but also California and New York to really lead in advancing aligned frameworks') and the Linero/TechNet quote ('would effectively be requiring private actors to make highly subjective determinations requiring AI safety compliance without established national standards...') verbatim as attributed (the article closes the TechNet quote before the source's trailing clause 'certifications, or clear regulatory guardrails' — a legitimate partial quotation of contiguous text, not a misquote). (4) source-3.html.gz (Chicago Sun-Times) — confirms the West Loop office signing location and, verbatim, all four quoted officials: Pritzker ('with that transformative potential comes catastrophic risk...' and the 'lack of leadership and foresight' line), AG Kwame Raoul ('one could argue $3 million is perhaps not enough' / 'the beginning step'), House Speaker Welch, D-Hillside ('a federal government that can't even meet people's basic needs, or the tech bros...'), and Sen. Edly-Allen, D-Grayslake, chief sponsor ('if we got social media wrong — and we did — we cannot afford to get AI wrong at an even greater scale'). (5) source-4.html.gz (Crowell & Moring client alert) — confirms enforcement authority vests in the Illinois attorney general, who may seek civil penalties for noncompliance. (6) source-5.html.gz (JURIST) — confirms New York's RAISE Act (June 2025, models 'that cost more than $100 million or exceed certain computational power') and California's Transparency in Frontier AI Act (September 2025, 'creates guardrails for the development of frontier AI models') verbatim as quoted. The article's framing of Illinois as the 'third state' to adopt frontier-AI safety standards is a reasonable, non-quoted synthesis from the two states JURIST documents as having acted before Illinois, not a fabricated claim. Four of the six domains (ilga.gov, capitolnewsillinois.com, chicago.suntimes.com, jurist.org) are not yet in config/source_allowlist.txt; I manually vetted each: ilga.gov is the Illinois General Assembly's own official bill-text and status system (a primary government source, directly analogous to already-allowlisted congress.gov); Capitol News Illinois is a nonpartisan, nonprofit Illinois statehouse news service funded by the Illinois Press Foundation and the Robert R. McCormick Foundation; the Chicago Sun-Times is one of Chicago's two major daily newspapers (chicagotribune.com is already allowlisted, so this is very likely an allowlist gap rather than a reliability concern); JURIST is an established legal-news and commentary service operated out of a law school since 1996. Per repository history (commits bd606be82/ea4569245/02a9b56ea), allowlist additions are handled as separate, deliberate maintainer commits rather than bundled into review commits, so I did not edit config/source_allowlist.txt here; I flag it below as a recommendation for a future maintenance pass.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: Every direct quote in the article (Pritzker x2, Raoul x2, Welch, Edly-Allen, Niedermeyer, Linero) appears verbatim in its cited snapshot. Every specific figure checked (10^26 FLOP compute threshold, $500M revenue threshold, 50-death/$1B catastrophic-risk definition, Jan 1 2028 audit start, 72-hour/24-hour incident windows, $1M/$3M penalty tiers, Jan 1 2027 effective date, Public Act 104-0538, 52-5-0 and 110-0-0 vote counts, NY RAISE Act and CA TFAIA dates and descriptions) traces exactly to its cited source. No hallucinated quotes, no fabricated specifics, and no misattribution were found across any of the six sources. This is one of the cleanest source-to-claim mappings I have reviewed.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and professional throughout. The article presents both supportive (OpenAI, Anthropic, bill sponsors) and critical (TechNet's subjective-determination objection, Raoul's own acknowledgment that the penalty may be insufficient) perspectives without editorializing. No AI self-reference.
